options.t: No; the court may grant a new trial only for the reason stated in the motion, since the parties framed the dispute.

stem: After a jury trial, judgment for Moss against Pine Ridge Co. is entered on Monday, March 2, 2026. On March 16, Pine Ridge moves for a new trial, supported by a juror's affidavit, and serves Moss that day. Moss files opposing affidavits on March 27. options.why: Does not apply. It governs a motion for a new trial after a nonjury trial; this was a jury trial.

options.t: Rule 59(c)

options.t: Rule 59(d)
options.why: Applies. The court may grant a timely motion for a reason not stated in it after notice and an opportunity to be heard.

options.t: Rule 59(b)
options.why: Applies. The motion came 14 days after entry, within the 28 days Rule 59(b) allows.

stem: Judgment is entered against Dale Roofing on Tuesday, January 13, 2026, after Dale's lawyer, through a calendaring error, missed the answer deadline. Dale first learns of the judgment in 2027 when it is served with a writ of execution. On Wednesday, February 3, 2027, Dale moves promptly under Rule 60(b)(1) to vacate the judgment for excusable neglect.
ask: Is Dale's motion timely?

options.t: Yes; Rule 60(c)(1) requires only a reasonable time, and Dale moved promptly after learning of the judgment.
options.why: Ignores the outer limit. For reasons (1), (2), and (3), Rule 60(c)(1) adds "no more than a year after the entry."

options.t: Yes; the one-year period runs from the date the movant learns of the judgment.
options.why: Wrong trigger. The year runs from entry of the judgment or order, not from discovery.

options.t: No; for reason (1), a Rule 60(b) motion must come within a year after entry, and Dale filed later.
options.why: Correct. Entry was January 13, 2026; the year ended January 13, 2027, three weeks before the motion.

options.t: No; a Rule 60(b) motion must be filed within 28 days after entry, as with a Rule 59 motion, so the motion is late.
options.why: Wrong clock. The 28-day periods are in Rule 59; Rule 60(c)(1) uses a reasonable time and, for reasons (1) to (3), one year.

explain: Rule 60(c)(1) requires every Rule 60(b) motion to be made within a reasonable time and, for reasons (1), (2), and (3), no more than a year after the entry of the judgment. Excusable neglect is reason (1). Entry was January 13, 2026, so a motion on February 3, 2027 is outside the year.

stem: After a bench trial, judgment for Ibis Foods is entered against Nolan on Monday, March 2, 2026. On Monday, June 1, 2026, Nolan finds an archived shipping log that contradicts a key finding. Nolan can show that, even with reasonable diligence, the log could not have been found in time to move for a new trial under Rule 59(b). Nolan moves for relief on June 8. Nothing suggests anyone hid the log.
ask: What is Nolan's best basis for relief?

options.t: Rule 60(b)(2), newly discovered evidence, if made within a reasonable time and within a year
options.why: Correct. The log fits reason (2) exactly, and June 8 is well within a year of the March 2 entry.

options.t: Rule 59(b); a motion for a new trial may be filed any time within a year after judgment is entered.
options.why: Wrong clock. Rule 59(b) allows 28 days after entry, which ended March 30.

options.t: Rule 60(b)(3), because the log proves that the court's finding was wrong on a central point.
options.why: Misreads (b)(3). It requires fraud, misrepresentation, or misconduct by an opposing party, and none is alleged.

options.t: Rule 60(b)(4), because new evidence makes the judgment void when it surfaces.
options.why: Evidence that the court was wrong does not make a judgment void; reason (4) is not triggered by new proof.

explain: Evidence that, with reasonable diligence, could not have been discovered in time to move for a new trial under Rule 59(b) is reason (2) under Rule 60(b). The Rule 59(b) period ended March 30, the log surfaced June 1, and the June 8 motion falls within the year allowed by Rule 60(c)(1).

stem: After a jury trial, judgment for Teal Inc. is entered against Arden on Monday, February 2, 2026. In June 2026, Arden learns that Teal's CEO knowingly gave false deposition and trial testimony about the contract's terms. Arden moves under Rule 60(b)(3) on July 6, 2026. Teal opposes, arguing that perjury at trial is "intrinsic" fraud, which cannot support relief.
ask: Is Teal's argument correct?

options.t: Yes; Rule 60(b)(3) reaches only extrinsic fraud, such as keeping a party away from the court itself.
options.why: The text covers fraud "whether previously called intrinsic or extrinsic."

options.t: Yes; false testimony can be raised only by a motion for a new trial under Rule 59(b).
options.why: Rule 60(b)(3) separately covers fraud and misconduct; Rule 59(b) is not the exclusive route.

options.t: No, but Arden must show the fraud was committed by the court rather than by a party.
options.why: Reverses the rule. Reason (3) concerns fraud or misconduct by an opposing party.

options.t: No; Rule 60(b)(3) reaches fraud or misconduct by an opposing party, whether intrinsic or extrinsic.
options.why: Correct. The rule text dissolves the intrinsic/extrinsic distinction, and the motion is within a year of entry.

explain: Rule 60(b)(3) allows relief for "fraud (whether previously called intrinsic or extrinsic), misrepresentation, or misconduct by an opposing party." Perjury by the opposing party's CEO fits, and a July 6 motion is within the year permitted by Rule 60(c)(1) for reason (3). Teal's intrinsic-fraud argument fails on the text.

stem: Judgment is entered against Kemp on Monday, March 2, 2026. In September 2027, nineteen months later, and promptly after learning of the judgment, Kemp moves to vacate under Rule 60(b)(4). The court concludes that the judgment is void. The plaintiff, Loom Corp., argues that the motion is time-barred because Rule 60(b) motions must be made within a year of entry.
ask: Is Kemp's motion time-barred?

options.t: Yes; every Rule 60(b) motion must be made within a year after entry of the judgment.
options.why: The year limit applies only to reasons (1), (2), and (3), not to reason (4).

options.t: No; the one-year cap applies only to reasons (1) to (3), so (b)(4) needs only a reasonable time.
options.why: Correct. Kemp moved promptly after learning of the judgment, which meets the reasonable-time requirement.

options.t: No; a motion that a judgment is void is subject to no timing requirement of any kind.
options.why: Overstates the rule. Every Rule 60(b) motion must be made within a reasonable time.

options.t: Yes; a motion attacking a judgment must be filed within 28 days after its entry, under Rule 59(e).
options.why: Wrong rule. Rule 59(e) governs motions to alter or amend; Rule 60(b)(4) is governed by Rule 60(c)(1).

explain: Rule 60(c)(1) requires all Rule 60(b) motions to be made within a reasonable time, and only reasons (1), (2), and (3) carry the additional one-year cap. A motion that the judgment is void under (b)(4), made promptly on learning of it, is not barred by the passage of 19 months.

stem: A $25,000 judgment is entered against Vance Motors on Monday, March 2, 2026. Two weeks later, the plaintiff, Reyes, signs a written release of the judgment in exchange for Vance's payment. Months later, Reyes's new lawyer, unaware of the release, applies for a writ of execution. Vance asks the court for relief from the judgment.
ask: Which provision of Rule 60(b) best fits Vance's request?

options.t: Rule 60(b)(1), mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect
options.why: Does not fit. The ground here is that the judgment has been released, which has its own reason.

options.t: Rule 60(b)(5), the judgment has been satisfied or released
options.why: Correct. Reyes released the judgment, which is exactly reason (5).

options.t: Rule 60(b)(6), any other reason that justifies relief
options.why: The catch-all is for other reasons. A released judgment is specifically covered by reason (5).

options.t: Rule 60(b)(4), the judgment is void
options.why: The judgment was valid when entered; a later release does not make it void.

explain: Reason (5) of Rule 60(b) applies when "the judgment has been satisfied, released, or discharged." Reyes's written release in exchange for payment fits that language, so Vance should move under Rule 60(b)(5), within a reasonable time.

stem: Judgment for Brandt against Hollis Co. was entered on March 2, 2020. In 2026, Hollis believes it has grounds to be relieved of the judgment and, rather than moving in the original case, files a new independent action to set the judgment aside. Brandt moves to dismiss, arguing that relief from a judgment may be sought only by a Rule 60(b) motion, subject to Rule 60(c)(1)'s time limits, and that Rule 60(e) abolished independent actions.
ask: Does Rule 60 bar Hollis's independent action?

options.t: Yes; Rule 60(b) is the exclusive route to relief from a judgment, and its one-year and reasonable-time limits have run.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 60(d)(1) says the rule does not limit a court's power to entertain an independent action.

options.t: Yes; Rule 60(e) abolishes independent actions along with bills of review.
options.why: Misreads 60(e), which abolishes bills of review and certain writs, not independent actions preserved by 60(d)(1).

options.t: No, but only if the court of appeals first gives leave to file the action.
options.why: Invents a requirement. Rule 60(d)(1) does not mention leave of any court.

options.t: No; Rule 60(d)(1) preserves the court's power to entertain an independent action for relief from a judgment.
options.why: Correct. The 60(c)(1) limits govern a motion under 60(b), not an independent action.

explain: Rule 60(d)(1) provides that the rule does not limit a court's power to entertain an independent action to relieve a party from a judgment. Rule 60(c)(1)'s time limits apply to "a motion under Rule 60(b)," and Rule 60(e) abolishes only bills of review and certain writs. Rule 60 therefore does not bar the action.

stem: A judgment entered on Monday, March 2, 2026 recites damages of $48,000, although the jury's verdict was $84,000; the clerk transposed the digits. In November 2026, with no motion pending and no appeal taken, the judge notices the error and, without notice to the parties, signs an order correcting the amount to $84,000. ask: Is the order valid under Rule 60?

options.t: Yes; the court may correct a clerical mistake whenever found, on motion or on its own, without notice.
options.why: Correct. A transposition by the clerk is a clerical mistake, and no appeal is pending.

options.t: No; a clerical mistake may be corrected only on a party's motion, never by the court on its own.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 60(a) lets the court act "on motion or on its own."

options.t: No; corrections must be made within 28 days after entry, as with a Rule 59(e) motion to alter or amend.
options.why: Wrong clock. Rule 60(a) permits correction whenever the mistake is found.

options.t: Yes, but only after the court gives the parties notice and an opportunity to be heard on the correction.
options.why: Adds a requirement. Rule 60(a) says the court may act "with or without notice."

explain: Rule 60(a) lets the court correct a clerical mistake in a judgment "whenever one is found," on motion or on its own, with or without notice. The transposed digits are a clerical mistake, no appeal had been taken, and the correction is valid.

options.t: Yes; Rule 60(a) lets the court correct a clerical mistake whenever one is found, even during an appeal.

options.why: Correct. That is the limit Rule 60(a) places on correcting a mistake while an appeal is pending.

options.t: Yes, but only with the consent of both parties.

cites.quote: The motion does not affect the judgment's finality or suspend its operation.
Except as provided in Rule 62(c) and (d), execution on a judgment and proceedings to enforce it are stayed for 30 days after its entry, unless the court orders otherwise.

stem: Judgment for $60,000 is entered against Ferro Works on Monday, March 2, 2026. On Tuesday, May 5, 2026, Ferro files a motion under Rule 60(b)(1). The next day the plaintiff, Kline, serves a writ of execution on Ferro's bank account. Ferro argues that its pending Rule 60(b) motion suspends the judgment's operation. No bond has been posted, the court has issued no stay, and the court has not ruled on the motion.
ask: Is Ferro correct?

options.t: Yes; filing a Rule 60(b) motion automatically stays enforcement until the court rules on it, however long that takes.
options.why: Contradicted by Rule 60(c)(2): the motion does not suspend the judgment's operation.

options.t: Yes; a Rule 60(b) motion suspends the judgment for 30 days under Rule 62(a).
options.why: Rule 62(a)'s 30-day stay runs from entry of the judgment, not from filing a Rule 60(b) motion.

options.t: No; a Rule 60(b) motion does not suspend the judgment, and the 30-day automatic stay expired April 1.
options.why: Correct. Ferro needed a bond under Rule 62(b) or a court order to stay enforcement.

options.t: No; the motion suspends execution only for 28 days, the Rule 59 period.
options.why: Invents a 28-day suspension. Rule 60(c)(2) provides no suspension at all.

explain: Rule 60(c)(2) provides that a Rule 60(b) motion "does not affect the judgment's finality or suspend its operation." The Rule 62(a) automatic stay ran 30 days from the March 2 entry and expired April 1. With no bond or order, Kline may enforce the judgment while the motion is pending.

stem: Judgment for Ames against Boll Co. is entered on Monday, January 12, 2026. Boll pays the judgment in full in February 2026. In April 2027, Ames, through a new lawyer, obtains a writ of execution anyway. Boll then moves for relief and asks the court (1) to declare the judgment satisfied, (2) to correct the caption, which misspells Boll's name, and (3) to vacate the judgment because Boll's former lawyer missed the answer deadline through a calendaring error. The motion is filed more than a year after entry.
ask: Which provisions may the court use to grant Boll relief on these requests? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 60(a)
options.why: Applies. A misspelled name in the caption is a clerical mistake that may be corrected whenever found.

options.t: Rule 60(b)(1)
options.why: Unavailable. A missed deadline from a calendaring error is excusable neglect, but reason (1) must be invoked within a year of entry.

options.t: Rule 60(b)(5)
options.why: Applies. Full payment means the judgment has been satisfied, and (b)(5) is not subject to the one-year cap.

options.t: Rule 59(e)
options.why: Unavailable. A motion to alter or amend must be filed within 28 days of entry.

options.t: Rule 60(b)(4)
options.why: Does not apply. Nothing in the facts suggests the judgment is void.

options.t: Rule 60(b)(3)
options.why: Does not apply. No fraud, misrepresentation, or misconduct by Ames is described.

explain: The caption error is a clerical mistake correctable under Rule 60(a) whenever found. Full payment satisfies the judgment under Rule 60(b)(5), which needs only a reasonable time. Reason (1) for the missed deadline is cut off by Rule 60(c)(1)'s one-year limit, and Rule 59(e)'s 28 days passed long ago.

The order is titled "Final Judgment on Count I" but contains no determination about delay. On June 1, before Count II is tried, Cruz presents new evidence and asks the court to reinstate Count I.
ask: May the court revise its ruling on Count I?

options.t: Yes; absent an express no-just-reason-for-delay determination, the order may be revised before judgment on all claims.
options.why: Correct. The title is irrelevant, and no judgment has adjudicated both counts.

options.t: No; once an order is labeled a final judgment, it can be revised only under Rule 60(b), whatever the court did or did not find.

options.why: Invents a consent requirement. Rule 54(b) has none.

stem: Tran sues two defendants, Orbit LLC and Pace Inc., on the same contract. On Monday, March 2, 2026, the court dismisses all claims against Orbit, expressly determines that there is no just reason for delay, and directs entry of final judgment for Orbit. ask: Is Tran correct?

options.t: Yes; no judgment can be final until all claims against all parties are resolved, however the court words its order.
options.why: Rule 54(b) allows a final judgment as to fewer than all parties on an express no-just-reason-for-delay determination.

options.t: Yes; the court needed Tran's consent to direct entry of final judgment against only one of the two defendants.
options.why: Invents a consent requirement. Rule 54(b) turns on the court's express determination.

options.t: No; but only because Orbit and Pace are both liable on the same claim, which keeps the claims linked.

options.t: No; Rule 54(b) permits final judgment for Orbit alone because the court expressly found no just reason for delay.
options.why: Correct. The court made that determination for Orbit.

explain: When multiple parties are involved, Rule 54(b) lets the court direct entry of final judgment as to fewer than all parties only if it expressly determines that there is no just reason for delay. The court made that determination, so the judgment for Orbit is final despite the pending claims against Pace.

cites.quote: A default judgment must not differ in kind from, or exceed in amount, what is demanded in the pleadings.

stem: Marsh sues Lyle for $50,000 in damages for breach of a lease; the complaint demands that amount and no more. Lyle never responds, and the clerk enters Lyle's default. ask: What is the most the court may award in the default judgment?

options.t: $120,000, because Marsh proved the higher amount of damages.
options.why: Ignores the limit. A default judgment must not exceed in amount what is demanded in the pleadings.

options.t: $50,000, because a default judgment cannot exceed the amount demanded in the pleadings.
options.why: Correct. Rule 54(c) caps a default judgment at the demand.

options.t: $85,000, the midpoint, because the court may split the difference.
options.why: No such rule. Rule 54(c) sets the demand as the ceiling.

options.t: There is no maximum; Rule 54(c) restricts only the kind of relief awarded, not the amount of it.
options.why: Wrong. The text says the judgment must not differ in kind from, "or exceed in amount," the demand.

explain: Rule 54(c) provides that a default judgment "must not differ in kind from, or exceed in amount, what is demanded in the pleadings." Marsh demanded $50,000 and never amended, so the court may award no more than $50,000 on default.

stem: Judgment for Pike against Quartz Mining is entered on Monday, March 2, 2026. A federal statute entitles the prevailing party to attorney's fees, and no statute or court order sets a different time for a fee motion. Pike's lawyer wants to file the fee motion on the last day permitted.
ask: By what date must Pike file the motion for attorney's fees?

options.t: March 9, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Seven days is the review window for the clerk's taxation of costs, not the fee-motion deadline.

options.t: March 16, 2026

options.t: March 30, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Twenty-eight days is the Rule 59 period, not the Rule 54(d)(2) period.

stem: After a bench trial on a federal-question claim, judgment is entered for Reed against Slate Co. on Monday, March 2, 2026. A federal statute allows the prevailing party to recover attorney's fees. Reed files a bill of costs for filing and copying fees with the clerk. The clerk gives notice on March 10 that costs will be taxed on March 24. Slate may want the court to review the clerk's taxation, and Reed plans to claim attorney's fees. The case involves one claim and two parties, and no default occurred.
ask: Which provisions of Rule 54 govern these events? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 54(b)
options.why: Does not apply. The action has one claim and the judgment ends it; no partial final judgment is involved.

options.t: Rule 54(c)
options.why: Does not apply. It limits default judgments, and the case was tried.

options.t: Rule 54(d)(1)
options.why: Applies. Costs other than fees go to the prevailing party, and the clerk taxes them on 14 days' notice, with court review on motion served within the next 7 days.

options.t: Rule 54(d)(2)(A)
options.why: Applies. A claim for statutory attorney's fees must be made by motion.

options.why: Does not apply. It exempts claims for fees as sanctions, and Reed's claim rests on a fee statute.

The statutory fee claim is made by motion under Rule 54(d)(2)(A), filed within 14 days after entry under Rule 54(d)(2)(B)(i).

cites.quote: When a party against whom a judgment for affirmative relief is sought has failed to plead or otherwise defend, and that failure is shown by affidavit or otherwise, the clerk must enter the party's default.

stem: Park sues Hale Co. and serves the summons and complaint on March 2, 2026. Sixty days pass and Hale does not answer, move, or otherwise respond. Park files an affidavit showing Hale's failure to plead or otherwise defend and asks that Hale's default be entered. Park's lawyer is unsure whether the judge or the clerk acts.
ask: Who must enter Hale's default?

options.t: Only the judge, after a hearing on the failure to respond.
options.why: Rule 55(a) assigns the entry of default to the clerk, and no hearing is required.

options.t: The clerk, but only after Park serves Hale with written notice 7 days before.
options.why: The 7-day notice is a Rule 55(b)(2) requirement for default judgment hearings, not for entry of default.

options.t: The judge, who may enter the default only after Park moves for a default judgment.
options.why: Reverses the sequence. The default is entered first under Rule 55(a); judgment comes under Rule 55(b).

options.t: The clerk must enter it, because Hale's failure to defend is shown by affidavit.
options.why: Correct. Rule 55(a) says the clerk "must" enter the default.

explain: Rule 55(a) provides that when a party has failed to plead or otherwise defend, and the failure is shown by affidavit or otherwise, "the clerk must enter the party's default." Park's affidavit shows Hale's failure, so the clerk acts; no judge or notice is needed at this stage.

stem: Vista Bank sues Dunn, an adult, on a promissory note for $18,400, a sum that can be made certain by computation from the note's terms. Dunn is properly served but never appears, and the clerk enters Dunn's default. Vista asks the clerk to enter judgment for the amount due plus costs and files an affidavit showing the amount due.
ask: Who may enter the default judgment?

options.t: The clerk, who must enter judgment for that amount and costs on Vista's request.
options.why: Correct. The claim is a sum made certain by computation, and Dunn is an adult who did not appear.

options.t: Only the court, after a hearing and 7 days' written notice to Dunn.
options.why: That is the Rule 55(b)(2) path for claims not within (b)(1); Dunn never appeared and the claim is a sum certain.

options.t: The court, because a default judgment is always a matter for the judge's discretion.
options.why: Wrong. Under Rule 55(b)(1) the clerk "must enter judgment" on a sum-certain claim against a defaulted adult who did not appear.

options.t: The clerk, but only if Dunn consents in writing.
options.why: Invents a consent requirement. Rule 55(b)(1) requires the plaintiff's request and affidavit.

explain: Rule 55(b)(1) requires the clerk, on the plaintiff's request with an affidavit showing the amount due, to enter judgment for the amount and costs when the claim is for a sum certain or one made certain by computation and the defendant defaulted for not appearing and is neither a minor nor an incompetent person.

cites.quote: If the party against whom a default judgment is sought has appeared personally or by a representative, that party or its representative must be served with written notice of the application at least 7 days before the hearing.

stem: Rowe sues Fisk Co. for unliquidated damages that require proof. Fisk appears through a lawyer early in the case but then stops defending, and the clerk enters its default. Rowe applies to the court for a default judgment, and the court sets the hearing for Wednesday, April 15, 2026. Rowe's lawyer wants to serve the required notice on the last permissible day.
ask: By what date must Fisk be served with written notice of Rowe's application?

options.t: April 1, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Fourteen days appears nowhere in Rule 55(b)(2).

options.t: April 10, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Five days is not the period in Rule 55(b)(2).

options.t: April 8, 2026
options.why: Correct. Rule 55(b)(2) requires service of written notice at least 7 days before the hearing; counting back from April 15 gives April 8.

options.t: April 14, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. One day's notice does not satisfy the 7-day requirement.

On March 16, Brook moves to set aside the entry of default, explaining that its insurer failed to forward the complaint. The plaintiff, Park, opposes, arguing that Brook must satisfy the grounds of Rule 60(b) because it seeks relief from a default.
ask: What standard governs Brook's motion?

options.t: The grounds in Rule 60(b), because any default requires relief under Rule 60(b).
options.why: Rule 55(c) distinguishes: Rule 60(b) governs setting aside a final default judgment, not an entry of default.

options.t: None; an entry of default cannot be set aside until judgment is entered.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 55(c) expressly allows the court to set aside an entry of default.

options.t: Good cause under Rule 55(c), because only an entry of default has been made.
options.why: Correct. Rule 55(c) lets the court set aside an entry of default for good cause; Rule 60(b) is for a final default judgment.

options.t: Rule 59(e), because the motion was filed within 28 days.
options.why: Wrong rule. No judgment exists to alter or amend, and Rule 55(c) addresses entry of default.

explain: Rule 55(c) distinguishes two situations: a court "may set aside an entry of default for good cause," but may set aside a "final default judgment under Rule 60(b)." Only the clerk's entry of default exists here, so the good-cause standard governs.

cites.quote: the clerk must enter the party's default.
In all other cases, the party must apply to the court for a default judgment.
The court may set aside an entry of default for good cause, and it may set aside a final default judgment under Rule 60(b).

stem: Jett sues Cray Corp., a private company, for unliquidated damages. Cray is served but never answers, and Jett files an affidavit showing that failure. Before any judgment, Cray's president appears, says the failure to answer resulted from an internal mix-up, and asks the court to undo the default. Jett wants a $200,000 default judgment without a hearing, though his claim is not for a sum certain and requires proof.
ask: Which provisions of Rule 55 apply? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 55(a)
options.why: Applies. Cray failed to plead or otherwise defend, shown by affidavit, so the clerk must enter its default.

options.t: Rule 55(b)(1)
options.why: Does not apply. The claim is unliquidated and not a sum certain, so the clerk cannot enter judgment.

options.t: Rule 55(d)
options.why: Does not apply. It concerns default judgments against the United States; Cray is a private company.

options.t: Rule 55(b)(2)
options.why: Applies. In all other cases the party must apply to the court for a default judgment.

options.t: Rule 55(c)
options.why: Applies. Before judgment, the court may set aside the entry of default for good cause.

explain: The clerk must enter Cray's default under Rule 55(a). Because the damages are not for a sum certain, Jett must apply to the court under Rule 55(b)(2). Cray's request to undo the entry of default, made before judgment, falls under Rule 55(c)'s good-cause standard. Rules 55(b)(1) and 55(d) are not triggered.

Holt argues that the denial is ineffective because it is not in a separate document.

options.t: No; a separate document is not required for an order disposing of a Rule 59 motion for a new trial.

stem: Following a jury trial, the jury returns a special verdict for Lund against Marlow Inc., answering written questions on liability and damages. The clerk, eager to close the file, prepares a judgment and proposes to sign and enter it without waiting for the judge. Marlow's lawyer objects.

options.t: The clerk may enter the judgment without the court's direction, as with any jury verdict.

cites.quote: The existence of another adequate remedy does not preclude a declaratory judgment that is otherwise appropriate.

explain: Rule 61 directs that "at every stage of the proceeding, the court must disregard all errors and defects that do not affect any party's substantial rights," and it reaches errors "by the court or a party." The omission affects no substantial right of Sloan, so the court disregards it.

cites.quote: Except as provided in Rule 62(c) and (d), execution on a judgment and proceedings to enforce it are stayed for 30 days after its entry, unless the court orders otherwise.

stem: Judgment for $90,000 is entered for Moll against Nest Co. on Monday, March 2, 2026. The court does not order otherwise, and no bond is posted. Moll's lawyer wants to know how long Nest is automatically protected from execution.
ask: What is the last day of the automatic stay of execution?

options.t: March 16, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Fourteen days is not the Rule 62(a) period.

options.t: March 30, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Twenty-eight days is the Rule 59 period, not the stay period.

options.t: April 1, 2026
options.why: Correct. Rule 62(a) stays execution for 30 days after entry; March 2 plus 30 days is Wednesday, April 1.
Wrong day count. Sixty days is not the Rule 62(a) period.

explain: Rule 62(a) stays execution and enforcement proceedings for 30 days after entry of the judgment unless the court orders otherwise. Counting 30 days from March 2 (excluding the day of entry) ends Wednesday, April 1, 2026.

cites.quote: The stay takes effect when the court approves the bond or other security and remains in effect for the time specified in the bond or other security.
At any time after judgment is entered, a party may obtain a stay by providing a bond or other security.

stem: Judgment for $75,000 is entered for Ulm against Heron Foods on Monday, March 2, 2026. On April 6, after the 30-day automatic stay has expired, Heron tenders a bond to the clerk and asks for a stay. The court approves the bond on April 10, and the bond is written to last 12 months. On April 8, Ulm serves a writ of execution on Heron's bank account.
ask: Is the April 8 execution subject to a stay by bond?

options.t: No; the stay took effect only when the court approved the bond on April 10, after the execution.
options.why: Correct. Heron's bond did not stay the April 8 execution.

options.t: Yes; the stay took effect when Heron tendered the bond on April 6.
options.why: Wrong trigger. Under Rule 62(b) the stay takes effect when the court approves the bond.

options.t: No; a stay by bond is available only during the 30-day automatic stay, which expired before Heron acted.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 62(b) permits a bond at any time after judgment is entered.

options.t: Yes; any tendered bond stays execution automatically for 30 days.
options.why: Invents a stay. Rule 62(b) requires court approval, and the 30-day stay is Rule 62(a).

explain: Rule 62(b) allows a party to obtain a stay by bond at any time after judgment is entered, but the stay "takes effect when the court approves the bond." Approval came April 10, two days after Ulm's April 8 execution, which the automatic stay (expired April 1) no longer protected.

cites.quote: Unless the court orders otherwise, the following are not stayed after being entered, even if an appeal is taken:
Except as provided in Rule 62(c) and (d), execution on a judgment and proceedings to enforce it are stayed for 30 days after its entry, unless the court orders otherwise.

stem: After a bench trial, the court enters a final judgment on Monday, March 2, 2026 permanently enjoining Brack Co. from dumping waste in a river. The judgment is silent about any stay. On March 10, Brack announces that it will continue operating as before, arguing that all proceedings to enforce the judgment are automatically stayed for 30 days after entry under Rule 62(a).
ask: Is Brack correct?

options.t: Yes; Rule 62(a) stays enforcement of every kind of judgment, including an injunction, for 30 days after its entry.
options.why: Ignores the exception. Rule 62(a) applies "except as provided in Rule 62(c) and (d)."

options.t: Yes, but only if Brack posts security under Rule 65(c).
options.why: Wrong rule. Rule 65(c) concerns the movant's security for an injunction, not a stay of one.

options.t: No; an injunction judgment is stayed only after an appeal is taken.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 62(c) says it is not stayed after being entered "even if an appeal is taken."

options.t: No; Rule 62(a) excepts Rule 62(c), and an injunction judgment is not stayed unless the court orders so.
options.why: Correct. Rule 62(c)(1) removes the automatic stay for such judgments.

explain: Rule 62(a) is subject to Rule 62(c). Under Rule 62(c)(1), a final judgment in an action for an injunction is not stayed after entry, even if an appeal is taken, unless the court orders otherwise. Brack's reliance on the 30-day automatic stay fails.

cites.quote: While an appeal is pending from an interlocutory order or final judgment that grants, continues, modifies, refuses, dissolves, or refuses to dissolve or modify an injunction, the court may suspend, modify, restore, or grant an injunction on terms for bond or other terms that secure the opposing party's rights.

stem: The district court denies Lark Corp.'s motion for a preliminary injunction against Mead Inc., and Lark appeals from that interlocutory order. While the appeal is pending, Lark returns to the district court and asks it to grant an injunction pending appeal, offering to post security to protect Mead.
ask: May the district court grant the injunction?

options.t: No; the pending appeal strips the district court of all power over injunctions in the case until the appeal is finally resolved.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 62(d) preserves the court's power during such an appeal.

options.t: Yes; during an appeal from an order refusing an injunction, the court may grant one on terms securing Mead's rights.
options.why: Correct. Rule 62(d) covers an appeal from an order that refuses an injunction.

options.t: Yes, but only with leave of the court of appeals, which must first approve the injunction terms.
options.why: Invents a requirement. Rule 62(d) gives the district court this power on its own terms.

options.t: Yes, and it may do so without any terms for bond or security.
options.why: Ignores the condition. The injunction is granted on terms for bond or other terms that secure the opposing party's rights.

explain: Rule 62(d) provides that while an appeal is pending from an order that "refuses" an injunction, the court "may suspend, modify, restore, or grant an injunction on terms for bond or other terms that secure the opposing party's rights." The district court may grant the injunction on such terms.

cites.quote: If a timely motion is made for relief that the court lacks authority to grant because of an appeal that has been docketed and is pending, the court may:
state either that it would grant the motion if the court of appeals remands for that purpose or that the motion raises a substantial issue.

stem: Judgment for Ness against Tamm Co. is entered on Monday, March 2, 2026, and Tamm appeals; the appeal is docketed and pending. Tamm then timely moves in the district court for relief under Rule 60(b)(2), citing newly discovered evidence. Because of the pending appeal, the district court lacks authority to grant the motion, though the judge thinks it has merit.
ask: What may the district court do under Rule 62.1?

options.t: Grant the motion and vacate the judgment now.
options.why: Impossible. The premise is that the court lacks authority to grant relief while the appeal is pending.

options.t: State that it would grant the motion if the court of appeals remands for that purpose.
options.why: Correct. That is one of the three options in Rule 62.1(a).

options.t: Defer considering the motion only; it may neither deny it nor state how it would rule on remand.
options.why: Too narrow. Rule 62.1(a) lets the court defer, deny, or state how it would rule.

options.t: Dismiss the motion with prejudice, because it may do nothing else.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 62.1(a) lists defer, deny, or state; none is dismissal with prejudice by necessity.

explain: When a timely motion seeks relief the court lacks authority to grant because of a docketed, pending appeal, Rule 62.1(a) lets the court defer considering it, deny it, or state that it would grant the motion if the court of appeals remands or that the motion raises a substantial issue. The judge may so state.

cites.quote: In a hearing or a nonjury trial, the successor judge must, at a party's request, recall any witness whose testimony is material and disputed and who is available to testify again without undue burden.

stem: Judge Ames begins a nonjury trial between Taft and Lund Co. After four days of testimony, Judge Ames becomes seriously ill and cannot continue. Judge Beck certifies familiarity with the record and determines the case can be completed without prejudice to the parties. Lund asks Judge Beck to recall Wynn, a witness whose testimony was material and disputed and who is available to testify again without undue burden. Judge Beck says she can simply read the transcript.
ask: Must Judge Beck recall Wynn?

options.t: No; recall is entirely within the successor judge's discretion.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 63 says the successor judge "must" recall such a witness at a party's request.

options.t: No; a successor judge may never take over a trial that is already under way, and must start over.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 63 allows any other judge to proceed after certifying familiarity with the record.

options.t: Yes, but only if both parties request it.
options.why: Invents a requirement. Rule 63 requires only a party's request.

options.t: Yes; in a nonjury trial the successor judge must recall such a witness at a party's request.
options.why: Correct. Each of Rule 63's conditions is met.

explain: Rule 63 lets a successor judge proceed after certifying familiarity with the record and finding no prejudice. In a nonjury trial the successor "must, at a party's request, recall any witness whose testimony is material and disputed and who is available to testify again without undue burden." Wynn meets all conditions.

cites.quote: At the commencement of and throughout an action, every remedy is available that, under the law of the state where the court is located, provides for seizing a person or property to secure satisfaction of the potential judgment.

stem: Cask sues Dunmore in federal court in State X for $400,000 for unpaid goods. At the start of the case, Cask fears Dunmore will move his assets. State X law lets a plaintiff obtain attachment of a defendant's property at the commencement of an action to secure a potential judgment. No federal statute applies.
ask: May Cask obtain attachment in the federal action?

options.t: Yes; Rule 64(a) makes State X's seizure remedies available from the start of the federal action.
options.why: Correct. Rule 64(a) incorporates the law of the state where the court sits, absent a governing federal statute.

options.t: No; attachment is available only after judgment is entered, under Rule 69, and never while the action is still pending.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 64(a) makes state seizure remedies available "at the commencement of and throughout an action."

options.t: No; Rule 65 injunctions are the only pre-judgment remedy in federal court.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 64 separately makes state-law seizure remedies available.

options.t: Yes, but only after Cask first wins a preliminary injunction.
options.why: Invents a precondition. Rule 64(a) attaches none.

explain: Rule 64(a) makes available, at commencement and throughout the action, every remedy that the law of the state where the court is located provides for seizing a person or property to secure satisfaction of the potential judgment, unless a federal statute governs. Attachment is listed in Rule 64(b), so Cask may seek it.

cites.quote: The remedies available under this rule include the following—however designated and regardless of whether state procedure requires an independent action:

stem: In a federal action in State Y, Fisk seeks a pre-judgment garnishment of Moro's bank account. State Y law would allow garnishment only by filing a separate lawsuit for that purpose, not by motion in the main case. No federal statute applies. Moro argues that Fisk therefore cannot obtain garnishment in the pending federal action.
ask: Is Moro correct?

options.t: Yes; a federal court must follow State Y's requirement that garnishment be sought in a separate independent action.
options.why: Rule 64(b) makes the listed remedies available "regardless of whether state procedure requires an independent action."

options.t: No; garnishment is not one of the remedies available under Rule 64.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 64(b) lists garnishment.

options.t: No; Rule 64 makes garnishment available regardless of whether state procedure requires an independent action.
options.why: Correct. Fisk may seek it in the pending action.

options.t: Yes; garnishment is available only after judgment.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 64(a) reaches remedies at the commencement of and throughout the action.

explain: Rule 64(b) lists garnishment among the available remedies "however designated and regardless of whether state procedure requires an independent action." State Y's separate-suit requirement therefore does not stop Fisk from seeking garnishment by motion in the pending federal action.

cites.quote: The court may issue a preliminary injunction only on notice to the adverse party.

stem: Gale Co. sues Fenn Inc. to stop Fenn's use of a trade name and moves for a preliminary injunction. Gale's lawyer, who has the phone number of Fenn's lawyer, asks the court to grant the preliminary injunction today without telling Fenn, saying that Gale expects to lose business.
ask: May the court issue a preliminary injunction without notice to Fenn?

options.t: Yes, if Gale's affidavit shows immediate and irreparable injury before Fenn can be heard.
options.why: Conflates two rules. That showing supports a temporary restraining order without notice under Rule 65(b), not a preliminary injunction.

options.t: Yes, if Gale's lawyer certifies in writing the efforts made to give notice.
options.why: Same conflation. The certification is a Rule 65(b)(1)(B) requirement for a TRO without notice.

options.t: No; the court may issue a preliminary injunction only on notice to the adverse party.
options.why: Correct. Rule 65(a)(1) allows no preliminary injunction without notice.

options.t: No, unless Gale first consolidates the hearing with the trial on the merits.
options.why: Wrong. Consolidation under Rule 65(a)(2) is optional and does not dispense with notice.

explain: Rule 65(a)(1) allows a preliminary injunction "only on notice to the adverse party." The no-notice route in Rule 65(b) is limited to temporary restraining orders. Gale cannot obtain a preliminary injunction without telling Fenn.

cites.quote: The order expires at the time after entry—not to exceed 14 days—that the court sets, unless before that time the court, for good cause, extends it for a like period or the adverse party consents to a longer extension.

stem: On Monday, March 2, 2026, the court issues a temporary restraining order against Zed Co. without notice, on a verified complaint showing immediate and irreparable injury and counsel's written certification of efforts to give notice. The order states its date and hour and the reasons, but provides that it will remain in effect for 30 days. Zed has not consented to any extension.
ask: Is the 30-day duration permitted?

options.t: No; it expires at the time the court sets, not to exceed 14 days, unless properly extended or Zed consents.
options.why: Correct. Neither exception has occurred.

options.t: Yes; no limit applies once the court finds irreparable injury and states its reasons in the order.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 65(b)(2) caps a no-notice TRO at 14 days absent a proper extension or consent.

options.t: No; the order may last no more than 10 days.
options.why: Wrong day count. The period is 14 days.

options.t: Yes; a TRO issued without notice may last until the preliminary-injunction hearing, whenever the court sets it.
options.why: Wrong. The expiration time may not exceed 14 days unless properly extended or Zed consents.

explain: Under Rule 65(b)(2), a TRO issued without notice expires at the time the court sets, "not to exceed 14 days," unless the court, for good cause, extends it for a like period before it expires, or the adverse party consents to a longer extension. A 30-day term with no consent is not permitted.

cites.quote: The United States, its officers, and its agencies are not required to give security.

stem: The United States, through a federal agency, sues Varo Chemical Co. to stop certain discharges and moves for a preliminary injunction. After a noticed hearing, the court is prepared to grant it. Varo asks the court to require the agency to give security to pay costs and damages if Varo is found to have been wrongfully enjoined.
ask: Must the agency give security?

options.t: Yes; Rule 65(c) requires security from every movant for a preliminary injunction.
options.why: Overlooks the last sentence of Rule 65(c), which excepts the United States.

options.t: Yes, but only if the adverse party asks for it, as Varo has.
options.why: Invents a request requirement and ignores the exception.

options.t: Yes; the exemption covers only a temporary restraining order, not a preliminary injunction.
options.why: Wrong. The exemption covers preliminary injunctions and TROs alike.

options.t: No; the United States, its officers, and its agencies are not required to give security.
options.why: Correct. Rule 65(c) says so in terms.

explain: Rule 65(c) requires a movant to give security before a court issues a preliminary injunction or TRO, but "the United States, its officers, and its agencies are not required to give security." The agency need not give security despite Varo's request.

cites.quote: The order binds only the following who receive actual notice of it by personal service or otherwise:
the parties' officers, agents, servants, employees, and attorneys; and

stem: The court enjoins Orion Corp. from shipping a product. Cole, a warehouse employee of Orion who is not named in the order, learns of the injunction from his supervisor's email the same day and ships the product anyway. Cole argues he is not bound because he was not a named party and was never personally served.
ask: Is Cole bound by the injunction?

options.t: No; the order binds only the parties named in it.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 65(d)(2)(B) also binds a party's employees who receive actual notice.

options.t: Yes; the order binds an employee of a party who receives actual notice of it.
options.why: Correct. Cole is Orion's employee and had actual notice by email.

options.t: No; only persons served with the order personally are bound.
options.why: Wrong. Actual notice "by personal service or otherwise" suffices.

options.t: Yes, but only if Cole is shown to be in active concert with Orion's attorneys.
options.why: Misreads the structure. Employees are bound under (d)(2)(B) on actual notice; active concert is a separate category.

explain: Rule 65(d)(2) binds the parties; the parties' officers, agents, servants, employees, and attorneys; and persons in active concert with them, but only those who receive actual notice "by personal service or otherwise." Cole is an Orion employee with actual notice, so he is bound.

cites.quote: The court may issue a temporary restraining order without written or oral notice to the adverse party or its attorney only if:
On 2 days' notice to the party who obtained the order without notice—or on shorter notice set by the court—the adverse party may appear and move to dissolve or modify the order.

The court may issue a preliminary injunction or a temporary restraining order only if the movant gives security in an amount that the court considers proper to pay the costs and damages sustained by any party found to have been wrongfully enjoined or restrained.

stem: Ross Labs sues Vale Corp. and, with a verified complaint, moves for a temporary restraining order without notice, asserting immediate irreparable injury before Vale can be heard. Ross's attorney certifies in writing her efforts to notify Vale and why notice should not be required. The court issues the order at 4:15 p.m. on Tuesday, March 3, 2026, after Ross gives security in an amount the court sets. Vale learns of the order the next morning and wants to appear and move to dissolve it.
ask: Which provisions of Rule 65 apply to these events? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 65(a)(2)
options.why: Does not apply. It concerns consolidating a preliminary-injunction hearing with trial; none is requested.

options.t: Rule 65(c)
options.why: Applies. A TRO may issue only if the movant gives security in an amount the court considers proper, and Ross did.

options.t: Rule 65(f)
options.why: Does not apply. It concerns copyright-impoundment proceedings.

options.t: Rule 65(b)(1)
options.why: Applies. A TRO without notice needs an affidavit or verified complaint showing immediate irreparable injury and the attorney's written certification.

options.t: Rule 65(e)(1)
options.why: Does not apply. It preserves federal statutes about employer-employee actions, and none is involved.

options.t: Rule 65(b)(4)
options.why: Applies. On 2 days' notice to Ross, or shorter notice set by the court, Vale may appear and move to dissolve or modify the order.

explain: The no-notice TRO satisfies Rule 65(b)(1) (verified complaint and attorney certification), requires security under Rule 65(c), and exposes the order to a dissolution motion by Vale on 2 days' notice under Rule 65(b)(4). Rules 65(a)(2), 65(e)(1), and 65(f) have no connection to the facts.

cites.quote: a party—on notice to every other party and by leave of court—may deposit with the court all or part of the money or thing, whether or not that party claims any of it.

stem: Hart Insurance holds $20,000 in policy proceeds claimed by two rivals, Ivy and Joss, in a federal action in which Ivy seeks a money judgment against Hart. Hart claims none of the money and wants to deposit it with the court. Hart's lawyer plans simply to hand the check to the clerk.
ask: What must Hart do to deposit the money?

options.t: Nothing more; any party may deposit funds with the clerk as of right, with no notice or order needed.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 67(a) requires notice to every other party and leave of court.

options.t: Give notice to every other party and get leave of court, then deliver the deposit order to the clerk.
options.why: Correct. That is the Rule 67(a) procedure.

options.t: Nothing; Hart cannot deposit because it claims none of the money.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 67(a) allows a deposit "whether or not that party claims any of it."

options.t: Wait until judgment is entered; deposit is available only after judgment has fixed who is entitled to the money.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 67(a) applies while part of the relief sought is a money judgment or a sum of money.

explain: Under Rule 67(a), a party seeking a money judgment or disposition of a sum of money may, "on notice to every other party and by leave of court," deposit the money with the court, "whether or not that party claims any of it," and must deliver a copy of the order permitting deposit to the clerk.

cites.quote: At least 14 days before the date set for trial, a party defending against a claim may serve on an opposing party an offer to allow judgment on specified terms, with the costs then accrued.

stem: Rainier sues Cobalt Inc. for breach of contract. Trial is set for Monday, April 20, 2026. Cobalt, the defending party, wants to serve an offer to allow judgment on specified terms, with the costs then accrued, and wants to do so on the last day the rule permits.
ask: What is the last day on which Cobalt may serve the offer?

options.t: April 13, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Seven days before trial is not the Rule 68(a) cutoff.

options.t: April 17, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Three days before trial is not the Rule 68(a) cutoff.

options.t: March 30, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Twenty-one days is not the Rule 68(a) period.

options.t: April 6, 2026
options.why: Correct. Rule 68(a) requires service at least 14 days before the date set for trial; April 20 minus 14 days is Monday, April 6.

explain: Rule 68(a) allows a defending party to serve an offer of judgment "at least 14 days before the date set for trial." Counting back 14 days from Monday, April 20, 2026 gives Monday, April 6, 2026.

cites.quote: If, within 14 days after being served, the opposing party serves written notice accepting the offer, either party may then file the offer and notice of acceptance, plus proof of service. The clerk must then enter judgment.

stem: Cobalt serves a timely Rule 68 offer to allow judgment against it for $30,000 plus costs then accrued. Within 10 days after being served, Rainier serves written notice accepting the offer. Cobalt's lawyer insists that the judge must first approve any judgment on the offer and that Rainier's acceptance came too early.
ask: What happens next under Rule 68(a)?

options.t: Either party may file the papers, and the clerk must then enter judgment.
options.why: Correct. Acceptance within 14 days after service triggers this procedure.

options.t: The case goes to trial, because an acceptance requires the court's approval.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 68(a) directs the clerk to enter judgment.

options.t: Only Cobalt may file the papers, and the court then decides whether to enter judgment.
options.why: Wrong. Either party may file, and the clerk must enter judgment.

options.t: The acceptance is void because the offeree must wait the full 14 days before accepting.
options.why: Misreads the period. Fourteen days is the outside limit for acceptance, not a waiting period.

explain: Rule 68(a) gives the offeree 14 days after service to serve written notice of acceptance. Rainier did so on day 10. Either party may then file the offer, notice of acceptance, and proof of service, and "the clerk must then enter judgment." No court approval is required, and early acceptance is valid.

cites.quote: If the judgment that the offeree finally obtains is not more favorable than the unaccepted offer, the offeree must pay the costs incurred after the offer was made.

stem: Cobalt serves a timely Rule 68 offer to allow judgment against it for $50,000 plus costs then accrued. Rainier does not accept within 14 days, and the case is tried. The final judgment for Rainier is $42,000, counting all costs accrued before the offer. Costs of $12,000 were incurred after the offer was made.
ask: What does Rule 68(d) require?

options.t: Rainier must pay all costs of both sides, including those incurred before the offer.
options.why: Overreaches. Rule 68(d) shifts only the costs incurred after the offer was made.

options.t: Nothing; Rule 68(d) applies only if the offeree loses outright.
options.why: Wrong. It applies whenever the judgment is not more favorable than the offer.

options.t: Rainier must pay the costs incurred after the offer was made.
options.why: Correct. The judgment finally obtained was not more favorable than the unaccepted offer.

options.t: Cobalt must pay the costs incurred after the offer, because Rainier prevailed.
options.why: Reverses the shift. Rule 68(d) puts the post-offer costs on the offeree who rejected.

explain: Rule 68(d) provides that if the judgment the offeree finally obtains "is not more favorable than the unaccepted offer, the offeree must pay the costs incurred after the offer was made." Rainier's $42,000 judgment is less favorable than the $50,000 offer, so Rainier bears the post-offer costs.

cites.quote: It must be served within a reasonable time—but at least 14 days—before the date set for a hearing to determine the extent of liability.

stem: In Hoff's suit against Zenith Corp., the court determines that Zenith is liable to Hoff, but the extent of Zenith's liability remains to be decided. A hearing on the extent of liability is set for Monday, June 15, 2026. Zenith, the party held liable, wants to make an offer of judgment and to serve it within a reasonable time and on the last day the rule permits.
ask: What is the last day on which Zenith may serve the offer?

options.t: June 8, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Seven days before the hearing does not satisfy the 14-day minimum.
Wrong day count. Twenty-one days is not the Rule 68(c) minimum.

options.t: June 1, 2026
options.why: Correct. Rule 68(c) requires service at least 14 days before the hearing date; June 15 minus 14 days is Monday, June 1.
Wrong day count. Three days before the hearing does not satisfy the 14-day minimum.

explain: When liability has been determined but its extent remains to be decided, Rule 68(c) lets the party held liable make an offer of judgment, to be served "within a reasonable time—but at least 14 days—before the date set for a hearing" on the extent of liability. Fourteen days before June 15 is June 1.

cites.quote: Evidence of an unaccepted offer is not admissible except in a proceeding to determine costs.
If the judgment that the offeree finally obtains is not more favorable than the unaccepted offer, the offeree must pay the costs incurred after the offer was made.
Unless a federal statute, these rules, or a court order provides otherwise, costs—other than attorney's fees—should be allowed to the prevailing party.

stem: Pike sues Orsa Co. Orsa serves a timely offer to allow judgment for $50,000 plus costs then accrued. Pike lets 14 days pass without responding. At trial, Pike's lawyer tells the jury that Orsa offered $50,000, arguing that this shows Orsa knew it was liable. Pike wins a judgment of $40,000, including costs accrued before the offer. The court must decide the evidence objection and who bears costs, including those incurred before the offer.
ask: Which provisions govern the evidence objection and the allocation of costs? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 68(c)
options.why: Does not apply. It concerns offers after liability has been determined; no such separate determination occurred.

options.t: Rule 54(c)
options.why: Does not apply. It limits default judgments, and this case was tried.

options.t: Rule 68(d)
options.why: Applies. The judgment finally obtained is not more favorable than the unaccepted offer, so Pike pays the costs incurred after the offer.
Does not apply. It sets the deadline for a fee motion, which neither question concerns.

options.t: Rule 68(b)
options.why: Applies. An unaccepted offer is inadmissible except in a proceeding to determine costs, so the jury should not hear it.

options.t: Rule 54(d)(1)
options.why: Applies. Absent a rule providing otherwise, the prevailing party gets costs, which governs the costs incurred before the offer.

explain: Rule 68(b) bars evidence of an unaccepted offer except in a costs proceeding, so the jury should not have heard it. Because the $40,000 judgment is not more favorable than the offer, Rule 68(d) shifts post-offer costs to Pike. Costs before the offer follow Rule 54(d)(1): they go to the prevailing party.

cites.quote: A defendant who did not answer before removal must answer or present other defenses or objections under these rules within the longest of these periods:
7 days after the notice of removal is filed.

stem: Lane sues Vim Corp. in state court. Vim is served with the summons and complaint on Monday, March 2, 2026, and has not answered. On Friday, March 20, 2026, Vim files a notice of removal to federal court. No court order sets a different schedule.
ask: By what date must Vim answer or present other defenses or objections?

options.t: March 27, 2026
options.why: Correct. Seven days after the March 20 notice of removal is the longest of the three periods, which also include March 23.

options.t: March 23, 2026
options.why: This is the 21-day date from service, but a shorter period does not control; the rule gives the longest of the periods.

options.t: April 3, 2026
options.why: Wrong day count. Fourteen days after removal is not a Rule 81(c)(2) period.

options.t: April 10, 2026
options.why: Wrong trigger. Twenty-one days runs from service, not from the notice of removal.

explain: Rule 81(c)(2) gives a defendant that had not answered the longest of: 21 days after receiving the initial pleading, 21 days after being served with the summons, or 7 days after the notice of removal is filed. The first two end March 23; the third ends Friday, March 27, the longest.

cites.quote: A defendant who did not answer before removal must answer or present other defenses or objections under these rules within the longest of these periods:

ask: Must Elm replead?

options.t: Yes; within 7 days after the notice of removal is filed.
options.why: The 7-day period applies to a defendant who had not answered before removal.

options.why: Correct. Rule 81(c)(2) says so.

options.why: Wrong trigger and wrong rule. Repleading is unnecessary absent a court order.

options.t: No, but only if Day consents.

explain: Rule 81(c)(2) provides that "after removal, repleading is unnecessary unless the court orders it." Elm answered in state court, so it need not file a new answer, and the time periods for answering apply only to a defendant who did not answer before removal.

After removal, repleading is unnecessary unless the court orders it.
A party who, before removal, expressly demanded a jury trial in accordance with state law need not renew the demand after removal.

stem: Pike sues Orco in state court and, as state law allows, expressly demands a jury trial there. Orco is served with the summons and complaint on Monday, March 2, 2026, but files no answer. On Friday, March 20, 2026, Orco removes the case. In federal court, Pike's lawyer asks (1) whether the Federal Rules now govern the case, (2) when Orco must respond, and whether repleading is needed, and (3) whether Pike must renew her jury demand. No court order addresses any of these points.
ask: Which provisions of Rule 81(c) resolve these questions? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 81(a)(2)
options.why: Does not apply. It concerns bankruptcy proceedings, and this is an ordinary removed civil action.

options.t: Rule 81(c)(3)(B)
options.why: Does not apply. It gives 14 days to demand a jury to a party that did not expressly demand one in state court; Pike did.

options.t: Rule 81(c)(1)
options.why: Applies. The Federal Rules apply to a civil action after it is removed from a state court.

options.t: Rule 81(b)
options.why: Does not apply. It abolishes scire facias and mandamus, which are not involved.

options.t: Rule 81(c)(2)
options.why: Applies. It governs further pleading and when a defendant that had not answered must respond.

options.t: Rule 81(c)(3)(A)
options.why: Applies. A party who expressly demanded a jury trial under state law need not renew the demand after removal.

explain: Rule 81(c)(1) makes the Federal Rules applicable after removal. Rule 81(c)(2) governs repleading and Orco's time to respond. Rule 81(c)(3)(A) excuses Pike from renewing her state-law jury demand. Rule 81(c)(3)(B) applies only where no express demand was made, and Rules 81(a)(2) and 81(b) are irrelevant.

cites.quote: A money judgment is enforced by a writ of execution, unless the court directs otherwise. stem: Seller wins a $30,000 money judgment in a federal court in State Z against Doyle, and the 30-day automatic stay expires. Seller wants to reach Doyle's equipment. No federal statute addresses the procedure for execution, and the court has not directed otherwise. Seller's lawyer is unsure whose procedure governs.
ask: How is the judgment enforced, and whose procedure governs?

options.t: By writ of execution, with a procedure the Federal Rules fully set out, displacing state law.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 69(a)(1) defers to state procedure, subject to any federal statute.

options.t: By contempt only; money judgments cannot be enforced by execution in federal court.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 69(a)(1) says a money judgment is enforced by a writ of execution.

options.t: By writ of execution, with the procedure of the state where the equipment was bought.
options.why: Wrong state. The procedure is that of the state where the court is located.

options.t: By writ of execution, with the procedure of State Z, where the court is located.
options.why: Correct. Rule 69(a)(1) so provides, absent a governing federal statute.

explain: Rule 69(a)(1) provides that a money judgment is enforced by a writ of execution unless the court directs otherwise, and that execution procedure "must accord with the procedure of the state where the court is located, but a federal statute governs to the extent it applies." State Z procedure governs.

cites.quote: If a judgment requires a party to convey land, to deliver a deed or other document, or to perform any other specific act and the party fails to comply within the time specified, the court may order the act to be done—at the disobedient party's expense—by another person appointed by the court.

stem: A federal court enters judgment requiring Garvey to execute and deliver a deed to Hale within 20 days. Garvey refuses. The land is in the district. Hale asks the court to have the deed executed without further delay and without first seeking a contempt order.
ask: What may the court do under Rule 70?

options.t: Order another person, appointed by the court, to execute the deed at Garvey's expense.
options.why: Correct. Rule 70(a) authorizes this when a party fails to comply within the time specified.

options.t: Nothing; a court cannot act in place of a party who disobeys a judgment that requires a specific act.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 70(a) authorizes the court to have the act done by another person.

options.t: Order Hale to execute the deed in Garvey's name at Hale's own expense.
options.why: Wrong person and wrong payer. The court appoints another person and the act is at the disobedient party's expense.

options.t: Act only after first holding Garvey in contempt.
options.why: Contempt is an additional power under Rule 70(e), not a prerequisite.

explain: Rule 70(a) provides that if a party fails to deliver a deed or perform a specific act within the time specified, the court may order the act done "at the disobedient party's expense—by another person appointed by the court," and the act then has the same effect as if done by the party. Contempt (Rule 70(e)) is also available but not required.

cites.quote: A party may not assign as error a defect in the order not timely objected to.
A party may serve and file objections to the order within 14 days after being served with a copy.

stem: A magistrate judge, to whom a nondispositive discovery dispute was referred to hear and decide, issues a written order on Monday, March 2, 2026, and the clerk serves a copy on Cass that day. Cass disagrees with the ruling but files nothing for 30 days. At the final pretrial conference, Cass asks the district judge to set aside the order, arguing it was erroneous.
ask: May Cass assign the defect in the magistrate judge's order as error?

options.t: Yes; objections to a magistrate judge's nondispositive order may be raised at any time before final judgment.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 72(a) requires objections within 14 days after being served.

options.t: Yes, but only if Cass first obtains the magistrate judge's permission to object late.
options.why: Invents a permission mechanism. Rule 72(a) bars assigning as error a defect not timely objected to.

options.t: No; a party may not assign as error a defect not timely objected to, and objections were due within 14 days.
options.why: Correct. Cass filed nothing in 14 days.

options.t: No; but only because Cass failed to arrange for a transcript of the proceeding.
options.why: Wrong ground. The bar rests on the failure to object timely.

explain: Under Rule 72(a), a party may serve and file objections to a magistrate judge's nondispositive order within 14 days after being served, and "may not assign as error a defect in the order not timely objected to." Cass objected on day 30 or later, so the objection is barred.

cites.quote: A district judge, magistrate judge, or other court official may remind the parties of the magistrate judge's availability, but must also advise them that they are free to withhold consent without adverse substantive consequences.

stem: At a pretrial conference, the district judge tells counsel that a magistrate judge is available to try the case if the parties consent. Pleased at how it would clear her docket, she adds that she would "think well" of parties who consent. She says nothing about whether the parties are free to decline.
ask: What does Rule 73(b)(2) require of the judge?

options.t: She may not mention the magistrate judge's availability to the parties at any time before they file consent.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 73(b)(2) permits a reminder.

options.t: She may remind them and need say nothing more, because consent is handled through the clerk's written notice to the parties.
options.why: Wrong. A reminder must be accompanied by the advice about withholding consent.

options.t: She may remind them, but must also advise them that they are free to withhold consent without adverse consequences.
options.why: Correct. She gave the reminder without the required advice.

options.t: She may proceed once the plaintiff alone consents.
options.why: Wrong. Rule 73(a) requires that all parties consent.

explain: Rule 73(b)(2) allows a judge to remind the parties of the magistrate judge's availability, but "must also advise them that they are free to withhold consent without adverse substantive consequences." The judge's remarks omitted the required advice and implied a benefit for consent.

cites.quote: But no hearing—other than one ex parte—may be conducted outside the district unless all the affected parties consent.

stem: The only active judge in a district sets a contested hearing on a motion for summary judgment at a hotel in a neighboring district, because that is where the judge will be that week. One party objects. No party has consented, and the hearing is not ex parte.
ask: May the judge hold the hearing there over the objection?

options.t: No; no hearing other than an ex parte one may be held outside the district unless all affected parties consent.
options.why: Correct. One party objects, so consent is lacking.

options.t: Yes; any proceeding other than a trial may be held anywhere inside or outside the district, even over a party's objection.
options.why: Ignores the proviso. A hearing outside the district, other than ex parte, needs all affected parties' consent.

options.t: No; every hearing must be held in a regular courtroom.
options.why: Overstates Rule 77(b). Only trials on the merits must be in open court, and other acts may occur in chambers.

options.t: Yes; the consent requirement applies only to trials.
options.why: Wrong. The consent requirement applies to hearings, with an exception for ex parte hearings.

explain: Rule 77(b) allows acts other than trials to be conducted by a judge anywhere inside or outside the district, "[b]ut no hearing—other than one ex parte—may be conducted outside the district unless all the affected parties consent." One party objects, so the judge may not hold the hearing there.

cites.quote: These rules do not extend or limit the jurisdiction of the district courts or the venue of actions in those courts.

stem: Gil, a citizen of State A, sues Hux, also a citizen of State A, in federal court on a state-law contract claim. No federal question is presented and no statute supplies jurisdiction. Gil argues that Rule 18(a), which lets a party join as many claims as it has against an opposing party, gives the court power to hear the dispute.
ask: Does Rule 18(a) supply the court with jurisdiction?

options.t: Yes; the joinder rules expand the court's jurisdiction to any claim properly joined.
options.why: Contradicted by Rule 82: the rules do not extend jurisdiction.

options.t: Yes, but only if Hux consents.
options.why: Consent cannot be a rules-based source of jurisdiction; Rule 82 says the rules do not extend it.

options.t: No, but only because Rule 82 limits venue, not jurisdiction.
options.why: Misreads Rule 82. It covers both jurisdiction and venue.

options.t: No; the Federal Rules do not extend or limit the district courts' jurisdiction.
options.why: Correct. Joinder under Rule 18(a) is a procedure, not a source of jurisdiction.

explain: Rule 82 provides that the Federal Rules "do not extend or limit the jurisdiction of the district courts or the venue of actions in those courts." Rule 18(a) governs which claims a party may join, not whether the court has subject-matter jurisdiction. With none shown, Rule 18(a) cannot supply it.

stem: Calder wins a federal judgment in State X against Dray for $90,000 plus an order requiring Dray to deliver a deed to a parcel. The 30-day stay has expired. Dray neither pays nor delivers the deed. Calder wants to levy on Dray's other property, learn where his assets are held by asking third parties questions, and have the deed delivered by someone else. No money is on deposit with the court, no receiver is involved, and no nonparty is bound.
ask: Which provisions support Calder's steps? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 69(a)(1)
options.why: Applies. A money judgment is enforced by a writ of execution under the procedure of the state where the court is located.

options.t: Rule 67(a)
options.why: Does not apply. It permits deposit of money with the court, and none is being deposited.

options.t: Rule 70(a)
options.why: Applies. When a party fails to deliver a deed, the court may have another person appointed by the court do the act at the disobedient party's expense.

options.t: Rule 66
options.why: Does not apply. It concerns actions in which a receiver is appointed or sued, and none is involved.

options.t: Rule 69(a)(2)
options.why: Applies. The judgment creditor may obtain discovery from any person in aid of judgment or execution.

options.t: Rule 71
options.why: Does not apply. It concerns enforcing orders for or against nonparties, and no nonparty is involved.

options.t: Rule 64(a)
